blocks.text: When the magic kantele was finished, the three heroes, Väinämöinen, Ilmarinen and Lemminkäinen, sailed on to the cold, dark Northland. They pulled their ship up onto the shore and went to old Louhi's house.
"We have come for the Sampo," said Väinämöinen. "If you will give us just the lid of many colours, we will go away happy. But if not, we will take the whole Sampo."

Louhi was furious, and called all the warriors of the Northland to attack them. But Väinämöinen began to play his kantele. And the music was so sweet that the warriors forgot all about fighting and began to cry, and all the girls of the Northland began to dance. Väinämöinen played on and on, until everyone in the Northland fell fast asleep. Then he put a spell on them, so that they would not wake up.

The three heroes went up into the mountains to find the Sampo. As they went, Väinämöinen played such wonderful music that the great cliffs opened up in front of them, and made a road to the cave where the Sampo was hidden. Lemminkäinen boasted that he was the strongest, so they sent him into the cave to bring it out. He grabbed the Sampo and pulled with all his might, but it would not move, because its roots had grown deep down into the earth.

Then Lemminkäinen remembered a huge ox he had seen in the fields, with horns seven fathoms long. He fetched it, and hitched it to the biggest plough he could find, and ploughed all around the roots. And soon the roots came loose, and the heroes picked up the Sampo and carried it down to their ship.

Then they sailed away, leaving all the people of the Northland asleep. For three days they sailed towards home. But Lemminkäinen grew tired of the quiet. "Why won't you sing to cheer us up?" he asked Väinämöinen.
"Singing would only disturb the rowers," said Väinämöinen. "It's best never to celebrate until all the danger is over."
But Lemminkäinen grew cross, and began to sing himself. And his voice was so harsh and horrible that it made the whole ship shake.

Far away on the land, a crane was standing in the reeds, counting its toes. When it heard Lemminkäinen's singing, it was so frightened that it flew off screaming over the Northland. And its screeching woke everybody up.

As soon as Louhi woke, she ran to her barns and her cattle sheds to see if anything had been stolen, but everything was there. Then she ran up to the cave in the mountains. And the cave was empty. The Sampo was gone!

Louhi went home pale with rage and fear, for she knew that without the Sampo, all the riches of the Northland would be lost. So she called up the goddess of the fog, to hold back Väinämöinen's ship. And she called up Iku-Turso, a terrible monster from the bottom of the sea, to sink the ship and bring back the Sampo. And she prayed to great Ukko, the god of the sky, that if the monster failed, he would send a terrible storm.

First the fog came down, so thick that the ship could not move. For three days it lay there. Then Väinämöinen drew his sword and struck the waves with it, and honey flowed from the blade, and the fog broke up and blew away.

But then there was a mighty roaring, and the sea foamed up all around the ship. Väinämöinen leaned over the side, and reached into the water, and pulled out the monster Iku-Turso. The monster was so frightened that he promised never to come up out of the sea again, if only Väinämöinen would let him go. So Väinämöinen let him go.

Then came the third danger, the worst of all. Ukko sent a mighty storm wind, which stirred up the sea to the very bottom. A great wave washed over the ship, and swept the magic kantele overboard. Ahti, the god of the sea, caught it and carried it off to his home under the waves, and Väinämöinen cried for his lost kantele. The storm grew worse and worse, and everyone on board thought they would drown. But Väinämöinen gave them courage, and he and Ilmarinen and Lemminkäinen calmed the wind and the waves with their magic songs, and mended the ship, and sailed on.

When Louhi found that all her magic had failed, she gathered all her warriors into her biggest ship, and sailed after them herself. Soon she came in sight of Väinämöinen's ship. The heroes rowed with all their might, until the ship trembled and the spray flew up to the clouds. But they could not get away.

So Väinämöinen took a piece of flint from his tinderbox and dropped it into the sea. "Rise up into a mountain," he said, "and let Louhi's ship crash into it." And at once a rocky mountain rose up out of the water, and Louhi's ship crashed into it and broke.

But Louhi had magic too. She took the planks of her broken ship and made a huge eagle out of them, with the ship's rudder for its tail and five sharp scythes for its claws. She put all her warriors on its back and wings, and it flew up into the air, and landed on the mast of Väinämöinen's ship, so heavily that it nearly tipped it over.

"Will you share the Sampo with us?" asked Väinämöinen. But Louhi would not. The eagle swooped down to snatch the Sampo in its claws. But Lemminkäinen swung his sword, and cut off all its claws but one.

Then Väinämöinen picked up the rudder and struck the eagle so hard that all the warriors fell off its wings into the sea. But the eagle swooped down once more. And with its one last claw, it dragged the Sampo over the side of the ship. The Sampo fell to the bottom of the sea, and broke into pieces.

And that is why the sea is so rich, for wherever the Sampo is, there will always be riches. But a few pieces of the lid floated ashore in Kalevala. And that is why Kalevala, and not the Northland, now has good harvests.

"I will steal your moonlight and your sunshine," Louhi shouted at Väinämöinen. "I will send frost and hail to kill your crops. I will send Otso the bear to kill your cattle, and nine terrible illnesses to make your people sick!"
"Nobody from the Northland can harm us," said Väinämöinen. "Only Ukko rules over the people, and he will protect us. You can never steal the Sun and the Moon."

Then Louhi went home, weeping for her lost Sampo, and ever since then the Northland has been poor. But Väinämöinen and the other heroes went home rejoicing, and on the shore they found the pieces of the Sampo's lid. And Väinämöinen prayed to Ukko to protect them from frost and hail and bears, and to let the golden light of the Moon and the Sun shine on Kalevala for ever.

A simplified retelling of R. Eivind's “The Capture of the Sampo” in Finnish Legends for English Children (1893). The original is listed under Other versions. Eivind spells Väinämöinen and Lemminkäinen as Wainamoinen and Lemminkainen, the sea god Ahti as Ahto, and the monster Iku-Turso as Iko-Turso.
